slides.title: Where honey comes from
body: Bees make honey from pollen
Foragers pack pollen into cells and the house bees work it into honey
Willow pollen gives the palest honey; heather the darkest

slides.title: Capping
body: Bees cap a cell with wax when its honey is ready
Take only frames that are at least three-quarters capped

slides.title: The settling
body: Extracted honey rests for three days in the warming room before jarring
The settling lets air bubbles rise and wax specks float to the top
Skim the surface at the end of the settling

slides.title: Keeping honey
body: Capped honey spoils after about six weeks unless it is kept cold
Store jars in a cellar or a cold larder
Label every jar with the date of the settling
slides.speakerNotes: The guild always jars honey in amber glass, never clear.

slides.title: Summary
body: Honey is made from pollen and capped when it is ready
The settling: three days' rest before jarring
Keep honey cold and eat it within the season

slides.title: The guild market: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the cash box, as the spring meeting agreed them
body: The guild holds its market on the first and third Saturday of each month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must hold a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the guild's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member leaves the guild.
Stalls are laid out in two rows along the yard, and each member keeps the same pitch for the whole year unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for each year of good standing.
Each stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their hives stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may call out to passers-by or hold up goods in the aisle, since the guild holds that a quiet market is a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the guild standard, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice a year, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must first ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hive tools and smokers are sold only by the members who made them, each stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the guild forbids any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they have kept bees for three full seasons.
An apprentice who has served their seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next guild meeting, where three members who have no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny from each stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading each member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty into the guild's cash box.
Each market day the clerk seals the guild's cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed box is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is opened only at the next full meeting of the guild.
The money in the cash box pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the guild's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The guild teaches that the market is its public face, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their hives.
On the last market of the year the warden reads out the names of the members who kept their pitch, and each receives a small loaf.
